title: Stress, strain and how materials fail

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the bar spring back to no stretch before yield but keep a permanent stretch after it, when you stretch it and let go.
interactive.title: The tensile test bar
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: The picture runs over seventeen small screens. The main picture is a steel test bar held in a testing machine's two grips. Two gauge marks on the bar sit 100 mm apart. The bar's section is an example 100 mm², about 11.3 mm across. You drag the lower grip down to stretch the bar. The stretch runs from 0 to 30 mm and opens at 0. The stretch is drawn far larger than to scale. An arrow at each grip shows the force on the bar. Readouts give the force in kN, the stress in N/mm² and the strain in per cent. The stress is the force in newtons ÷ the bar's first area, 100 mm². The strain is the stretch between the gauge marks ÷ 100 mm. So here the strain in per cent is the same number as the stretch in mm. Beside the bar, a dot runs along the stress-strain curve and draws the curve behind it. The curve is a sketch of a mild steel. Its straight start rises at 200 000 N/mm² for each whole unit of strain. That slope is steel's Young's modulus, labelled stiffness. It reaches an example yield strength of 250 N/mm² at 0.125% strain. That takes a force of 25 kN. Then it runs flat for a short step and rises in a gentle arch. It passes 360 N/mm² at 10%. It peaks at an example 400 N/mm² at 20%, a force of 40 kN. That peak is the tensile strength, labelled strength. Past the peak the bar draws in at one spot, into a neck. The stress falls to 320 N/mm², or 32 kN. The bar breaks at 30 mm. The first 0.5% of the strain axis is drawn far wider than the rest, so the straight start shows as a slope. You can let go anywhere. When you do, the dot runs back down a line parallel to the straight start until the force is zero. Before yield that line ends at zero, so the bar springs back to its first length. After yield it ends to the right of zero. The stretch then splits into two labelled parts, each in mm. One is the springback and the other is the permanent stretch. The springback is the stress at letting go ÷ 200 000, times the 100 mm between the marks. Let go at 10 mm and 360 N/mm² and the bar springs back 0.18 mm. It keeps 9.82 mm. Past the widened part, the squeezed axis makes the line back look upright. So a small zoomed box beside the bar draws the line back to one scale. There it is as steep as the straight start. Dragging again climbs the dot up that same line back to the curve. After the break, a button fits a new bar. Screen 1 shows the same 10 kN pull on a 20 mm bar and a 10 mm bar. The 20 mm bar has 314 mm² of section, so 31.8 N/mm². The 10 mm bar has a quarter of the area, 78.5 mm², and four times the stress, 127 N/mm². Screen 2 asks the stress from a 6 kN pull on a rod of 40 mm² section: 150 N/mm². One wrong pick is 6 kN, the force itself. The other is 0.0067 N/mm², the area ÷ the force. Screen 3 shows two plates pulled opposite ways, 5 kN each, joined by one 10 mm pin. The pin is cut across where the plates meet. Its section is 78.5 mm², so the shear stress is 5000 ÷ 78.5 = 63.7 N/mm². Screen 4 asks the shear stress in a key cut across over 8 mm by 40 mm, carrying 16 kN: 320 mm², so 50 N/mm². One wrong pick is 400 N/mm², from dividing by the 40 mm length only. The other is 0.05 N/mm², from leaving the force in kN. Screen 5 shows two steel bars at the same stress. The 1 m bar stretches 0.5 mm and the 2 m bar 1 mm. Both have a strain of 0.0005, or 0.05%. Screen 6 asks the strain of a 2.5 m rod stretched 1.5 mm: 0.0006. One wrong pick is 0.6, from millimetres ÷ metres. The other is 1.67, the length ÷ the stretch. Screen 7 brings in the test bar and its straight start. At 20 kN it reads 200 N/mm² and 0.1%, a 0.1 mm stretch. When you let go, it springs back to zero. Screen 8 asks the Young's modulus of an aluminium alloy bar. The bar reads 70 N/mm² at 0.1% strain. The answer is 70 000 N/mm², about a third of steel's. One wrong pick is 700 N/mm², from dividing by 0.1 instead of 0.001. The other is 70 N/mm², the stress itself, drawn as a flat red line at the 70 level. Screen 9 drags past yield and lets go, leaving a permanent stretch. A faint curve sketches a metal with no clear corner. It starts on the same straight line and bends over smoothly toward 320 N/mm². A dashed line starts at 0.2% strain and runs parallel to the straight start. It cuts the faint curve at about 282 N/mm², its yield strength by the offset rule. It meets the steel's sketch at 250 N/mm². Screen 10 asks what stretch stays after letting go at 10 mm and 360 N/mm²: 9.82 mm. One wrong pick is 0 mm, as if it all springs back. The other is 10 mm, as if none does. The zoomed box shows the answer's line back to one scale. Screen 11 drags on past the peak to the neck and the break. It labels stiffness as the slope and strength as the height. Screen 12 shows two sketched curves. A ductile one runs far, necks and breaks. A brittle one breaks soon after its straight start. The area under the ductile curve is shaded as its toughness. Screen 13 shows two sketched curves. Bar A is brittle, with the steeper straight start, and stops short at its break. Bar B is ductile, with the higher peak. It asks which is stiffer: A. Screen 14 shows the steel's curve. A dashed line marks an example working stress of 100 N/mm². So the factor of safety on yield is 250 ÷ 100 = 2.5. The test bar's safe working load is 100 × 100 mm² = 10 000 N, or 10 kN. Screen 15 shows a shaft bent a little by its load as it turns. End on, its keyway is marked. A trace shows that spot's stress swing from stretched to squeezed once every turn. A small crack at the keyway grows a little each turn. Screens 16 and 17 mix it all. Screen 16 asks the safe working load of a 20 mm bar. Its yield is 250 N/mm² and its factor of safety is 5. The answer is 15.7 kN. One wrong pick is 78.5 kN, with no factor. The other is 3.1 kN, divided by 5 twice. Screen 17 asks the stretch of a 3 m steel tie of 200 mm² carrying 20 kN: 1.5 mm. One wrong pick is 0.0015 mm, from leaving the force in kN. The other is 0.0005 mm, the strain with no length. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. A wrong pick is drawn, so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The curve is a sketch of one mild steel with example values. Real steels vary a lot. Many other metals have no flat step at yield. The first part of the strain axis is drawn far wider than the rest. Drawn to one scale, the straight start would look like a vertical line. The stress here is the force ÷ the bar's first area, as a test reports it. In the thinning neck the force is spread over less metal, so the stress there keeps rising. The bar is pulled slowly at room temperature. Speed, heat and cold change the curve. Fatigue is shown only as the shaft's stress swinging. How fast a crack grows, and how many turns it takes, are not shown. The faint rounded curve is a made-up sketch, not a measured metal. Hardness is only named. It is found by pressing a hard ball or point into the surface, a different test.

explain.text:
Any pull stretches a metal bar a little. Pull harder and it stays stretched, and harder still it breaks. A tensile test pulls a bar steadily to the break and records the force and the stretch all the way. Plotted as one curve, they show three different things: how stiff the metal is, where it starts to stretch for good, and how strong it is. A sling leg in tension carries just this kind of pull. Here is what that pull does to the metal.

The curve should belong to the metal, not to one bar. So take out the bar's size. A thicker bar spreads the same pull over more metal. So divide the force by the area of the bar's section. That is the [[stress]], in newtons per square millimetre. A 20 mm bar has 314 mm² of section. A 10 kN pull on it gives 31.8 N/mm². Stress is not a force. A 10 mm bar has a quarter of that area. The same 10 kN on it gives four times the stress, 127 N/mm². A pull acts along a bar. A shear load acts across a part instead. It slides one side of a cut past the other, as across a pin or a key. Its [[shear stress]] is the force ÷ the area of the cut.[^1] A 5 kN load across a 10 mm pin gives 63.7 N/mm². A longer bar stretches further under the same stress, because every millimetre of it stretches the same. So divide the stretch by the length. That is the [[strain]]. It is a length over a length, so it has no units. A 1 m bar stretched 0.5 mm has a strain of 0.0005, or 0.05%. A squeeze works the same way, with the stress and strain pushing instead of pulling.

At low stress, strain rises in step with stress, like a spring's load against its stretch. Take the load off and the bar springs back to its first length. The slope of that straight start is stress ÷ strain. It is called the elastic modulus. For a pull it is called [[Young's modulus]]. It is the metal's stiffness: how much stress it takes to stretch it a given amount. Steel's is about 200 000 N/mm². An aluminium alloy's is about a third of that, so the same stress stretches it about three times as far. Past a certain stress the line bends over, and the bar starts to stretch for good. That stress is the yield strength. Let go now and only part of the stretch springs back. That part is still the elastic stretch, with the same stiffness. So the bar gives back a strain of the stress ÷ Young's modulus. It comes back along a line parallel to the straight start. It keeps the rest. Many metals bend over without a clear corner. Their yield strength is usually taken as the stress that leaves 0.2% of permanent strain.[^2] Pull on and the stress climbs to a peak. That peak is the tensile strength. Past it, the bar thins at one spot into a neck. The neck loses area faster than the metal gets stronger, so the force it carries falls until it breaks. Stiffness is the slope of the straight start. Strength is the height of the peak. A metal can be stiff and weak, or springy and strong.

Mild steel is [[ductile]]. It stretches a long way and necks before it breaks. A [[brittle]] material, such as glass or a ceramic, breaks with hardly any permanent stretch. [[Toughness]] is the energy a material soaks up before it breaks. It is the area under its curve.[^3] So a ductile metal is usually the tougher one. [[Hardness]] is different again. It is how well a surface resists denting or scratching.

So a part is designed to run well below its yield strength. The factor of safety is the failing stress ÷ the working stress. The safe working load is the working stress × the area of the section. Even well below yield, a load that comes and goes can crack a part. At a tiny flaw or a sharp corner, such as a keyway, the stress is higher than in the rest of the part. A crack starts there and grows a little each cycle, until the part breaks. That is fatigue. A shaft bends a little under its load. As it turns, every spot on its surface feels this. Each spot is stretched as it passes one side, and squeezed as it passes the other. Fatigue is the most common way shafts fail. **Stiffness, yield and strength are three different things on one curve. Stiffness is the slope of its straight start. Yield is where it bends over. Strength is the height of its peak.**

analogy.text: Think of a resistor's ohms and its power rating. Its ohms are the slope of its volts-against-amps line: how many volts it drops for each amp. Young's modulus is the slope of the stress-strain line in the same way: how much stress for each bit of strain. The power rating is a separate limit you must not pass. Two 100 Ω resistors can be rated 0.25 W and 50 W. They have the same slope and very different limits. In the same way, two bars can be equally stiff and very different in strength.
analogy.breaks: A resistor pushed past its rating overheats and burns out. It keeps nothing like the permanent stretch a bar keeps after yield.

practice.text:
- Safe way first: never load a part past its safe working load. That figure already has the factor of safety in it. It is a limit, not a target.
- Find the area of the section in mm². For a round bar it is π × radius².
- Work out the stress: the force in newtons ÷ the area. Use newtons, not kN.
- For a pin or a key cut across, the shear stress is the force ÷ the area of the cut.
- Compare it with the metal's yield strength. For a part that must not bend for good, the factor of safety is the yield strength ÷ your stress.
- For the stretch below yield, divide the stress by Young's modulus to get the strain. Then multiply by the length in mm.
- On anything that turns or shakes, ask whether the load comes and goes. If it does, fatigue can set a safe stress well below yield.

**Rule of thumb:** half the diameter means a quarter of the area, so four times the stress. Steel stretches about 0.5 mm per metre at 100 N/mm².

**Worked example:** a 4 m steel tie rod, 16 mm across, carries 12 kN. Its area is π × 8² = 201 mm². The stress is 12 000 ÷ 201 = 59.7 N/mm². The strain is 59.7 ÷ 200 000 = 0.000298. So it stretches 0.000298 × 4000 = 1.19 mm. Say its steel yields at an example 250 N/mm². Then the factor of safety is 250 ÷ 59.7 = 4.2.

**Common mistakes**
- Treating a stress as a force. A stress is the force on each square millimetre.
- Dividing the area by the force instead of the force by the area.
- Using a strain in per cent as if it were a plain fraction. That puts the answer out by 100.
- Mixing up stiffness and strength. A stiff part stretches little. A strong part takes a big stress before it fails.
- Ignoring sharp corners such as a keyway. Fatigue cracks often start at them.
